idiom_name: map[key]memo with a struct key {rule, pos} and comma-ok lookup
implementation_notes: Go's built-in map accepts any comparable key, so the memo is map[key]memo with type key struct{ rule, pos int } - the Go blog recommends a single struct key over nested maps precisely because it removes the create-the-inner-map dance - and the two-value lookup (m, ok := p.memo[k]) is the hit test. The zero value of the stored struct cannot express 'not computed', so the memo struct carries an explicit fail bool and is written back on every miss, failures included. What replaces the classic memo-table object is that no such object exists: the table is a field, the rules are ordinary functions in a slice, and one wrapper method supplies the lookup/store pair. Maps are not safe for concurrent use, so a table shared by goroutines needs a mutex or one table per parse.
pitfalls: Maps are not safe for concurrent use: sharing one memo between goroutines is a data race - guard it with a mutex/RWMutex or keep one table per parse.
The memo holds *Node pointers, so a table that outlives the parse pins the whole tree and defeats the collector; drop or clear it when parsing finishes.
A struct key is copied on every lookup and only optimised away while it stays on the stack; a packed integer key is cheaper in hot loops when positions are bounded.
